pages.title: ASEAN introduction: the ASEAN way and human rights
pages.summary: ASEAN is the most successful regional organisation of developing countries, inspired by the EU, and has its own constitution, but follows the non-interfering ASEAN way instead of supranationalism. It is criticised for neglecting human rights (the Rohingya crisis in Myanmar is a challenge) and is divided over China.

pages.title: ASEAN divisions, achievements and its 1967 formation
pages.summary: ASEAN faces regional imbalance (the CLMV countries are least developed), political instability and unresolved border disputes. Its achievements include a nuclear weapon free zone, economic integration and the ASEAN Regional Forum, and it was formed in 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration with five original members.

pages.title: ASEAN milestones from 1971 to 2015
pages.summary: The milestones include ZOPFAN (1971), Bali Concord and the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation (1976), the Preferential Trading Agreement (1977), AFTA (1992), the ASEAN Regional Forum (1994), the nuclear weapon free zone (1995), ASEAN Charter (2007) and the 2015 declaration as a security community. The page also compares ASEAN's two summits a year with SAARC and SAPTA.

pages.title: ASEAN three pillars and India's growing partnership
pages.summary: ASEAN has economic, political-security and social-cultural pillars, and is the nucleus of security architecture and India's gateway to the Asia Pacific. India moved from overlooking ASEAN to sectoral dialogue partner in 1992, full dialogue partner in 1996, summit-level partner in 2002 and strategic partner in 2012.

pages.title: India-ASEAN ties, trade and reasons for Look East
pages.summary: ASEAN includes India in the Regional Forum, East Asia Summit and other initiatives, and trade rose from 9.4 bn dollars in 1990 to around 200 bn dollars, with an FTA in 2010 and a services FTA in 2015. Look East, started by PM Narasimha Rao, was driven by the collapse of the USSR, economic needs, China's rise and better India-US relations.

pages.title: Look East phases and announcement of Act East
pages.summary: Look East Phase I under Narasimha Rao stressed economic diplomacy, and Phase II under Vajpayee added strategic aims, bilateral ties, defence partnerships and Look East through the North East. The Act East Policy was announced in 2014 in Myanmar with a focus on culture, commerce and connectivity, and the MEA notified it in December 2015.

pages.title: Act East: wider scope and strategic focus
pages.summary: Act East expands focus from South East Asia to Asia Pacific and North East Asia, strengthening strategic partnerships with Japan and South Korea and engaging Mongolia, Vietnam, Singapore and even North Korea. It gives primary weight to strategic and maritime security, with an assertive stand on the South China Sea, LEMOA with the USA and India-Japan-USA naval exercises.

pages.title: Act East priorities and the rebranding debate
pages.summary: Act East prioritises North East development, infrastructure, connectivity, skill development, counter-terrorism and Indian initiatives such as Make in India, with special focus on CLMV countries. Most scholars see rebranding, but C Raja Mohan sees more in speed, scale and space, and Rajiv Bhatia lists five new features.

pages.title: Initiatives of the Modi government under Act East
pages.summary: Initiatives include upgraded strategic partnerships, the Forum for India Pacific Island Cooperation, the India-ASEAN plan of action 2016-20, invitations to the International Solar Alliance and Make in India, and faster physical and digital connectivity. The PM also coined NEZ for the North East, though security conditions there obstruct the vision.

pages.title: Conclusion and Mekong Ganga Cooperation
pages.summary: India is now present in all economic and security architectures in Asia-Pacific. The Mekong Ganga Cooperation, launched in 2000 at Vientiane, is an economic and strategic initiative to regain ground lost to China, built on people-to-people contact and four pillars: tourism, culture, education and transport and communication.

pages.title: MGC momentum, trilateral highway and Kaladan project
pages.summary: MGC languished due to India's domestic issues and Thailand's instability but gained momentum under Act East with a 2016-18 plan of action covering trade, IT and pharmaceuticals, plus extra lines of credit to CLMV countries. The India-Myanmar-Thailand trilateral highway and the Kaladan multi-modal project are noted, with a reminder to draw a map.

pages.title: Nalanda revival and APEC as open regionalism
pages.summary: Nalanda University is an example of reviving old linkages. APEC, set up in 1989 with 21 member economies, is open regionalism with minimal institutionalisation and voluntary pledges, includes both China and Taiwan, excludes India, and aims at border trade facilitation, supply chains and better business environment.

pages.title: APEC commitments and India's case for membership
pages.summary: APEC commitments are non-binding and decisions are by consensus, with Bogor goals adopted in 2014, and the grouping represents 2.8 bn people, 47% of global trade and 60% of global GDP. Membership is a Look East objective, and India's chances improved because the APEC moratorium ended, the business climate and GST improved and diplomatic efforts continue.

flashcards.front: How does the ASEAN way differ from the EU's approach to integration?
flashcards.back: The EU follows a supranational approach based on treaties, whereas ASEAN follows the ASEAN way based on principles similar to Panchsheel, especially non-interference in domestic affairs, though it has its own constitution.

flashcards.front: When and how was ASEAN formed, and who were the original members?
flashcards.back: It was formed in 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration with five original members: Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Philippines. Brunei and the CLMV countries joined later.

flashcards.front: Trace the stages of India's partnership with ASEAN.
flashcards.back: India became a sectoral dialogue partner in 1992, a full dialogue partner in 1996, a summit-level partner in 2002 and a strategic partner in 2012.

flashcards.front: Why did India adopt the Look East Policy?
flashcards.back: The USSR collapsed, the new economic policy needed trade while SAARC economies were protectionist, a rising China changed the strategic environment, and better India-US relations helped integration. Geography, culture and history also supported it.

flashcards.front: How did Look East Phase I differ from Phase II?
flashcards.back: Phase I under Narasimha Rao focused on economic diplomacy with ASEAN as the priority. Phase II under Vajpayee added a strategic dimension, moved beyond ASEAN to bilateral ties, built defence partnerships with countries like Vietnam and Malaysia, and promoted Look East through the North East.

flashcards.front: How does the Act East Policy differ from Look East according to the notes?
flashcards.back: Act East widens scope from South East Asia to Asia Pacific, with focus on North East Asia and partners like Japan and South Korea, and its primary focus is strategic, with emphasis on maritime security, the South China Sea and LEMOA with the USA.

flashcards.front: Is Act East merely rebranding? What do C Raja Mohan and Rajiv Bhatia say?
flashcards.back: Most scholars see rebranding. C Raja Mohan sees more because of the speed, scale and space of engagement, and Rajiv Bhatia lists five new features including tangible results, expanded geography, a shift to North East Asia, bolder defence expression and confidence in RCEP.

flashcards.front: What is the Mekong Ganga Cooperation and what are its four pillars?
flashcards.back: It is an economic and strategic initiative launched in 2000 at Vientiane to regain India's ground lost to China in the Mekong region. Its pillars are tourism, culture, education, and transport and communication.

flashcards.front: What does open regionalism mean in APEC and why does APEC use the term member economies?
flashcards.back: It means minimum institutionalisation with voluntary pledges according to capacity and non-binding commitments by consensus. APEC says member economies because both China and Taiwan are represented.

answers.question: Trace the evolution of India's Look East Policy into the Act East Policy. Is Act East only a rebranding?
answers.intro: India's Look East Policy began under Narasimha Rao as economic diplomacy with ASEAN. Over successive governments it became strategic, and the 2014 Act East Policy widened its geography and ambition, raising the debate over rebranding versus real change.
body: Origins: the USSR's collapse, new economic policy, protectionist SAARC economies, China's rise and improved India-US ties pushed India eastwards. Phase I under Narasimha Rao focused on economic diplomacy, Phase II under Vajpayee added strategic and defence ties and Look East through the North East.

Act East: announced in 2014 with culture, commerce and connectivity, it moves from South East Asia to Asia Pacific and North East Asia, with partners Japan, South Korea, Mongolia, Vietnam and Singapore.

Strategic content: maritime security, an assertive stand on the South China Sea, LEMOA with the USA and India-Japan-USA naval exercises, plus CLMV focus, Make in India, International Solar Alliance and North East development.

Debate: most scholars call it rebranding, but C Raja Mohan stresses unprecedented speed, scale and space, and Rajiv Bhatia lists five features, including tangible results, wider geography and bolder defence expression.
answers.conclusion: Act East builds on continuity but has added pace, strategic depth and wider geography. Its success will depend on delivering connectivity projects and resolving the security constraints in the North East.

answers.question: Evaluate ASEAN as a model of regional integration, noting its achievements and challenges.
answers.topic: ASEAN as a model of integration
answers.intro: ASEAN is the most successful regional organisation of developing countries, inspired by the EU but following its own ASEAN way. It has built peace and economic integration, yet faces divisions over China, human rights and uneven development.
body: Approach: unlike the EU's supranational method, the ASEAN way is based on principles like Panchsheel, especially non-interference. ASEAN has its own constitution (the 2007 Charter), whereas the EU manages with treaties, and works as a community with three pillars.

Achievements: formed in 1967 by Bangkok Declaration, it declared ZOPFAN (1971), signed the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation (1976), AFTA (1992), a nuclear weapon free zone (1995) and security community status in 2015.

Architecture: the ASEAN Regional Forum is the only security platform in Asia where arch rivals like India and Pakistan, or the two Koreas, can hold dialogue, and ASEAN contributes to peace in Asia as a whole.

Challenges: no effective human rights approach (the Rohingya crisis in Myanmar), division on China (Laos, Cambodia and the Philippines pro-China, Indonesia non-aligned), the underdeveloped CLMV countries, instability in Thailand and unsettled border disputes.
answers.conclusion: ASEAN is a successful model for developing regions in peace and economic integration, though its non-interference norm limits human rights action. Closing the CLMV development gap and managing the China question will determine its future.
